utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Good morning to you once more. Mr. Popovic, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. Mr. Beara, can you understand the proceedings in your own language? THE ACCUSED BEARA: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you follow the proceedings in your own language? THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, same question. THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Miletic, same question. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation. Yes, I can, but I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will repeat the same question to you. Are you receiving interpretation now? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And can you follow the proceedings in your own language, in other words? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gvero, same question to you. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is Peter McCloskey. Together with me today is Madam Prosecutor, Carla Del Ponte; and the attorneys from the Srebrenica Zepa trial team, Julian Nicholls, Nelson Thayer, Lada Soljan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. And good morning to you as well, Madam Del Ponte, and the rest of the team. Appearances for Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jelena Nikolic, and together with Mr. Stephane Bourgon and Bojan Stefanovic, our case manager, we represent Mr. Drago Nikolic.

utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Ivanovic, and good morning to you and your team. Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I, Peter Haynes, appear together with Mr. Djordje Sarapa for Vinko Pandurevic. We're assisted in court today by our case manager, Helena Kaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team, Mr. Haynes. So before we move ahead with the opening statement, Prosecution, are there any preliminaries? Yes, Madam Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the accused have not received the operative indictment which was filed on the 4th of August, 2006, in B/C/S.

utterances.text: What about the other accused? In other words, is yours an exception or does -- does it apply to each and every one of the accused? utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's being translation process. I will find out and I will get back you, to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll work on it, Madam Fauveau and other counsel, and we'll see to it that it's distributed without any undue delay. Any further preliminary matters? Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Judges. Mr. President, I would like at this time and before we proceed with the opening statement of the Prosecutor -- Prosecution, to present an oral joint motion for reconsideration of the decision issued by the Trial Chamber on Friday, the 18th of August, 2006. We are of the view, Mr. President, on behalf of all seven accused in this trial, that this motion must be heard before we proceed with the Prosecution's opening statement for a number of reasons, including the fact that the motion, of course, deals with all seven accused in this case. Secondly, the motion concerns the proceedings as a whole as well as the fairness of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon. If you're going to make submissions, we'll give you a time limit within which to make your submissions. We'll give equal time to the Prosecution to reply, and we will hand down our oral decision soon after, as soon as practicable, and then we can start. But if you're going to make submissions, you have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I will get straight to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This matter has been decided on in a written -- in an oral -- excuse me, in a written decision, and we would object, especially at this time, at this critical time, to any delay. If -- if this matter, if you think it should be discussed in court, I would request that any discussion be made at the end of the trial day and that we allow the Prosecutor to make her statement and -- and that I make -- begin my statement and then we handle this later. But this matter has been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but there is an intimation that the joint Defence teams would like to have the matter reconsidered. So let's hear what they have to say. You will be given every opportunity to reply, and then we'll hand down our decision soon after or as soon as practicable. But I can assure you the matter will be dealt with in a final manner this morning, within the next 20 minutes or so. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please restrict yourself to any submissions which are new and not those that we have already decided upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President. Mr. President, the legal basis for this motion is the Appeals Chamber decision of June 2006 in the Zigic case saying that a Trial Chamber may and has the power to reconsider its decision on the basis of either a change of circumstances or on the basis that the decision is erroneous and has caused a prejudice to the Defence. All Defence attorneys in this case, Mr. President, believe that both a delay of the aspects of this test are met in this case. Moving straight away to the situation of the change of circumstances. In the decision, the Trial Chamber said, recognised that the Prosecution had not fulfilled entirely its disclosure obligation. However, it did recognise that or maybe it was not satisfied that the partial non-disclosure by the Prosecution has denied the Defence the ability to prepare adequately for trial. The order said we will -- the Prosecution is to comply without delay with its disclosure obligation pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E) (iii), and the Prosecution is to provide the Defence before or by the commencement of trial proceedings with an update of its witnesses for August and September, which shall include a list of exhibits to be used with each. Under the heading "change in circumstances," I respectfully submit on behalf of all the accused the following: Firstly, the Prosecution has not provided the Defence as it was ordered to do a revised list of witnesses for August and September along with a list of exhibits to be used. Secondly, the Prosecution has not provided the Defence since the decision with any further disclosure of exhibits that it intends to offer at trial. Thirdly, the Prosecution has failed as ordered by the Trial Chamber on 30 June to file its proofing chart for all witnesses in this case by 18 August 2006, last Friday, as it was ordered to do. Fourthly, on 18 August the Prosecution filed a new motion, a new motion for three additional witnesses as well as 360 new documents to be added in this case. For sure, Mr. President, the Prosecution knew when it responded to the Defence motion that it was about to file 360 new documents and ask for three more witnesses. For sure, Mr. President, the Prosecution knew that it would not be able to file its proofing chart by Friday when it responded to the Defence motion. Fifthly, Mr. President, the Defence still has not received a full index indicating the material that is necessary or that is relevant for each of the witnesses in this case. Meaning that for each witness we have consistently been asking the Prosecution to provide us with what is the material, statements, interviews, prior testimonies, information reports, and any documents which may have been provided by each of the witnesses. This information, Mr. President, is required at this time, and it has not yet been provided. It is not for the Defence to look for this information. It is for the Prosecution to provide this information. Sixthly, Mr. President, the Defence has not yet received the information requested in order to make the Prosecution pre-trial brief a meaningful document. This was brought to the attention of the Prosecution in both some of the pre-trial briefs filed by the Defence as well as on 14 July during the pro forma beginning of this trial. We believe, Mr. President, that all of this is a change of circumstances that warrant a reconsideration of the motion. Under the heading "prejudice to the Defence," I will make it short and simply address two categories which need further emphasis; namely, the issue of the intercept material. 150 at least intercept material which have not yet been provided to the Defence in English. This material, Mr. President, for sure must have been reviewed and analysed by the Prosecution at some point, and in addition, it must have been reviewed by the lead trial attorney from the Prosecution. The Prosecution cannot deny that this material is important for its case, yet the Defence does not have it in English in order to prepare for this trial. Secondly, Mr. President, the issue of the operational logs. Both of these issues were addressed in our motion, and we are under the -- we respectfully submit that they have not been addressed sufficiently or considered in rendering the decision. These operational logs is a tool that will be absolutely required by both the Defence and the Trial Chamber alike, with a view to being able to understand better these witnesses. Looking at the prejudice, Mr. President, when we look at the missing material, when we look at the missing translations, when we look at the fact that we do not have the proofing chart order for 18 August, that we do not have a proper pre-trial brief, that we do not have an updated witness list, that we do not have a list of material for each witness, this, Mr. President, has hampered Defence preparations to a point where it is necessary to postpone the proceedings in this case. Now, we opened up in terms of our last submission, which was our reply, we said we will proceed this week with those two first witnesses. We will proceed with those -- with the opening statements if that is the wish of the Trial Chamber. However, before any further meaningful or witnesses which address a lot of exhibit testify before this Chamber, they should, Mr. President, at least ten days before we get all the material and the testimony of the first such witness. This is my five minutes. I would have much more to say, but in the gist, this is what the -- on behalf of all seven accused in this case we believe that there is a prejudice to the Defence and that there is a need to postpone the proceedings in this case. Maybe not for long, but what is important is the Prosecution must be in a position or must be -- must have a way to fulfil its obligation so that we can have this trial started on a firm and sound basis. Thank you, Mr. President, on behalf of all the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon, also for staying within the time limit. Mr. McCloskey, you have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, having this thrown at me like this I've tried to keep track of what he's saying, but it's difficult because he says he hasn't received the proofing chart. The proofing chart has been filed, and so I don't know what the problem is and I don't know what else is a problem that really is not in what he said, because the proofing chart is filed. The updated exhibit and witness list we have a stack right here ready to give to them. I had thought it had been given electronically, so I'd asked my co-counsel not to pass it out right at the hour. Apparently it's not been sent electronically but we have it, so it's here. The other matter, on the over 300 new documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the subject matter of an outstanding motion. I mean, if you deal with it very briefly in the same way it has been submitted or along the same lines it has been made reference to by Mr. Bourgon, okay. Otherwise, please go on to the next point. I mean, the idea is that -- this should -- the fact that there is this outstanding motion in itself should delay the commencement of the -- of the case. Do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that makes sense. If I could just mention so Your Honour is aware that -- why there is 300 some-odd new exhibits, very briefly. The Miletic trial brief surprised us where he denied any involvement in providing humanitarian aid. We had over 200 documents with his name on it that are pro forma convoy-type documents, not all of which have been translated. So out of an abundance of caution in response to the pre-trial brief, we've got those to the Defence as soon as we could. They're not all translated. So many of these documents are in response to pre-trial brief issues that we now are -- understand will be contested at trial. We've tried to avoid dumping enormous numbers of documents on the Defence early on in the exhibit list, and so we will hope to be adding as issues come up, not in a huge bulk. Frankly, the other issues he mentioned, the intercepts, the logs, I could discuss those at length, but we've discussed those in our brief. There's no need to, especially for the logs, to translate all the information in all the logs. We have translated the part that is much relevant. The intercepts we're doing our best to translate as quick as we can, and we've left the some 100, 150 as potentially relevant intercepts and I hope to perhaps cut off some of those intercepts as I get the translations. But our analyst said they appeared relevant, so out of an abundance of caution we've put those on our list. And that's the group we're talking about. I don't have any English translations that we're holding back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How soon will you be making use or do you anticipate you'll be making use of any of these intercepts or operational logs with witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Months and months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The guts of this case, the documents and the intercepts, it comes at the end of the case, and I think we've all tried to examine how long this will take, but probably not between 6 and 9 months down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's the most of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So we will have a very short break, three minutes, four minutes maximum, and we'll come back with a decision. Yes, I see both Mr. Bourgon and Madam Fauveau. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can have, please with your permission one minute to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There has been no proofing chart filed. The proofing chart, there was a proofing chart filed back in July but there was one segment for 18 of August which has not been filed, unless it was filed after hours on Friday, but we even checked with court management this morning. It has not been filed. The Miletic document deals with the Main Staff. This is joint criminal enterprise case. All accused in this case must review these documents. All we hear from the Prosecution is inadvertently abundance of caution, eleventh hour, avoiding dumping. It's a matter, Mr. President, of what message the Trial Chamber wants to send to the justice community to the judicial community in terms of can we start this trial on a firm basis, or do we just say time is the only thing that matters. Prosecution, you can do what you want. It doesn't matter as long as we get this trial going. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would be very grateful to the Prosecution if it could quote the brief I have filed, because the terms used by the Prosecutor are not quite the terms which we used in our pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Do you have any further comments, Mr. McCloskey, before we retire for our deliberations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a set of documents that have just been submitted that applied to my client among the 360. I'm not talking about documents that apply only to General Miletic. There are other documents that apply to other accused as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is, from my experience here over the last five years, that is something that continues, goes on and on and on throughout the entire trial. Documents keep arriving as they come to the surface, and we usually intervene when we are convinced that you need time to go through them before -- before you can proceed with the case, but let's see whether that's the case now. We will retire for a few minutes. We'll come back with our oral decision. Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.27 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber is seized of a joint Defence motion made this morning for reconsideration of its decision filed last Friday on another joint Defence motion for postponement of the commencement of the trial. This is our oral decision. We have heard oral submissions by parties. We have confirmed that the -- the proofing chart that was expected to be filed by last Friday was indeed filed, although it seems it has not been distributed. We consider the submission relating to the Prosecution request to add three witnesses and about 360 fresh exhibits to be the subject matter of an outstanding motion and should be dealt with as such in that motion and not as a reason for delaying the commencement of -- or the -- for postponing the commencement of the trial. Equally, we have heard confirmation from the Prosecution that the intercept material and operational logs will be made use of with witnesses at a much later stage in the proceedings. We do not consider any of the other so-called fresh circumstances mentioned this morning by Mr. Bourgon and others such as to warrant a postponement in the commencement of the trial. Consequently, we stand by our decision of last Friday, which denied the joint Defence motion for postponement -- for postponement of the commencement of proceedings, and we order that the proceedings in this trial be proceeded with forthwith. Thank you. Any further preliminary matters? I hear none. So, Madam Del Ponte, I take it you wanted the floor first before Mr. McCloskey. Go ahead. MS. DEL PONTE: Yes, Your Honours, Mr. President. Yes, indeed I would like to make a few brief opening remarks before Senior Trial Attorney Peter McCloskey addresses you. For those of us gathered here today, over a decade and nearly 2.000 kilometres removed from the events of Srebrenica in July 1995, it is difficult, if not impossible, to comprehend the scale of the horror inflicted on the inhabitants of the Srebrenica enclave. Words cannot convey the magnitude of the crimes committed and the suffering endured by the victims. For the survivors, the wounds have not yet heeled and the suffering continues. For many of them, it still feels like only yesterday that they were forcibly separated from their families and saw their loved ones taken away by armed soldiers, never to see them again. In most cases, never to learn what finally happened to them. Before the war, Srebrenica was known mainly for the local mining industry and for its health spas. The town was not particularly well known outside of the former Yugoslavia. In 1991, the population was approximately 75 per cent Muslim. Now, now, the name of Srebrenica is infamous. Srebrenica is invariably associated with the most heinous of crimes: Forcible transfer, mass murder, and genocide. It is beyond reasonable dispute that genocide and other crimes against humanity were committed in Srebrenica in July 1995. These terrible facts have been proven, have been proven in other trials held before this Tribunal. The facts of the forcible transfer of the population and the mass executions have also been painstakingly established by investigations and reports of the United Nations, human rights organisations, and governments. As just one example, let me read you a portion of the concluding paragraph of the 15 November 1999 report of the Secretary-General pursuant to General Assembly Resolution 53/35. The fall of Srebrenica, and I quote: "The body of this report sets out in meticulous, systematic, exhaustive and ultimately harrowing detail of the descent of Srebrenica into a horror without parallel in the history of Europe since the Second World War. I urge all concerned to study this report carefully and to let the facts speak for themselves. The men who have been charged with these crimes against humanity reminded the world, and in particular the United Nations, that evil exists in the world." Your Honours, the facts do indeed speak for themselves. Let me quickly discuss some of the key facts which are before and will be proven beyond reasonable doubt in this trial. In July 1995, the Bosnian Serb army, or VRS, implemented the final phase of a comprehensive criminal plan to permanently erase the Muslim population of Srebrenica. As is well known, the enclave fell to the VRS on 11 July 1995, after a brief military campaign. Within three days, in an atmosphere of utter terror, tens of thousands of citizens, women, children, and the elderly, were forcibly removed from the enclave by the VRS and Bosnian Serb police forces. What little the victims could carry they brought with them in bundles as they were loaded into overcrowded buses in the village of Potocari near Srebrenica. The separation of Potocari was captured by a Serb cameraman, and you will see scenes of these poor terrified people being forced from their homes. You will hear first-hand evidence of the fact that the men and boys gathered in Potocari were prevented by armed soldiers from entering the buses with their families. Instead, they were separated from their wives, mothers, sisters, and daughters. These men and boys, aged approximately 15 to 78, faced a far grimmer fate. After being separated from their families, they were confined in cramped detention facilities under brutal conditions. Their meager belongings were taken away from them, piled up, and burned. In the following weeks, VRS and police forces systematically murdered over 7.000 Muslim men and boys from the Srebrenica enclave. The victims included those separated from their families in Potocari, as well as thousands of men and boys who either surrendered or were captured as they tried to flee the enclave. These victims, civilians as well as soldiers who had set down their arms, were detained, murdered in firing squads and bulldozed into mass graves. Where are the victims of these mass executions today? Most of them remain together in mass primary or secondary graves hidden in the woods and buried beneath the fields. They lie together, many of them undoubtedly still bound by wire and blindfolds, for the evidence shows that many victims were bound with ligatures and blindfolded in order to make the murder easier for the executions. These were not, not deaths sustained as has been argued, in combat. And that is what this case is about, Your Honours. An entire population erased, women, children and the elderly forced from their homes; defenseless men and boys executed by firing squads, buried in mass graves, and then dug up and buried once again in an effort to conceal the truth from the world. But the lasting tragedy of Srebrenica, the leading legacy of this atrocity is with the families left behind. The women and children forced to live their lives deprived of their fathers, without their husbands, their brothers, their sons, their neighbours, their community gone. The continuing impact of these crimes on the Muslim population of Srebrenica was evident most recently at the ceremony last month in Potocari commemorating the 11th anniversary of the fall of Srebrenica. Thousands of mourners, mainly women, gathered there for the burial of still more victims at the memorial centre. At the ceremony, over 500 more victims of genocide were buried. They joined some 2.000 other victims in the ground of the cemetery at the memorial centre. However, all too many victims still await a proper burial. To date over 3.000 victims have been exhumed by the Office of the Prosecutor and the international community. They are stored anonymously in morgues, bearing tags, waiting for the identifications that in many cases may never be realised. For some of the survivors, a minority, there is at least the sense of certainty that comes when a missing loved one is finally found and identified. However, for far too many of the survivors there is not even this small measure of relief. The questions remain: What happened to my father, my husband, my son. Why was he killed? Where is he? What were his last moments like? Why did this happen to us? Let me review something said by one survivor, Witness DD, in previous Srebrenica trial about the loss of a child and how she still felt the pain years after he was taken from her in Potocari, and he remains among the missing. I quote: "As a mother, I still have hope. I just can't believe that this is true. How is it possible that a human being could do something like this, could destroy everything, could kill so many people? Just imagine this youngest boy I had, those little hands of his, how could they be dead? I imagine those hands picking strawberries, reading books, going to school, going on excursions. Every morning I wake up, I cover my eyes not to look at other children going to school and husbands going to work holding hands." The pain expressed in those words is felt by every survivor who still waits to learn of the fate of a loved one. Justice. Your Honours, the ceremony of Potocari was, of course, a ceremony of loss and grief, but it was also a ceremony of hope, hope for justice. And with justice, the hope for reconciliation between peoples. With justice comes the hope for a lasting peace. The surviving victims of these crimes yearn for justice, not revenge. There is a passage which the Grand Mufti of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mustafa Efendija Ceric, often states in his prayers and appeals to people to remember the crimes of Srebrenica and pray that they shall never be perpetrated again against any people. I would like to repeat it to you: "Revenge is not a Bosnian tradition. Revenge is not a Bosnian measure. The truth is our belief, and justice is our destiny." This trial is the next phase in bringing to justice those men most responsible for all of the crimes against humanity committed in Srebrenica and Zepa. There have been other trials concerned with the crimes in Srebrenica. These trials have exposed the truth and punished some of the guilty, but all of those individuals most responsible for this genocide, and indeed the other crimes committed in Srebrenica, have not yet been brought to justice. This trial is an important step towards that goal. These seven accused, Your Honours, officers, serving below Ratko Mladic and Zdravko Tolimir are among those most responsible, most responsible for the terrible crimes committed in Srebrenica as set forth in the indictment. The crimes that are the subject of this indictment in this case were committed with brutality, boldness, and impunity in equal measure. The separation of the women and children from the men and boys in Potocari and their forcible expulsion while the men and boys were detained awaiting execution took place in front of rolling television cameras. It was broadcast around the world as the crimes occurred, and of course you will see much of this video evidence during the course of the trial. It is right to recall as we start this trial that the ICTY was created in the face of continued and serious violation of international humanitarian law in the former Yugoslavia. This judicial institution is the product of one of the most important measures taken by the Security Council acting for all Member States of the United Nations to restore and maintain international peace and security. That is our collective mission, our responsibility and our contribution to peace and security, to bring to justice those individuals responsible for the most serious crimes known to humanity. The crimes that are the subject of this trial, genocide, the crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war are set forth in the indictment, and indeed all the crimes within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal are crimes of such a magnitude that they injure us all. These crimes are offences against the victims and all of human kind because they are of a scale that offend our deepest principle of human rights and human dignity. The trials before this Tribunal have proven that international law is not merely theory nor an abstract concept. International law is and must be a fully functioning system to protect our values and regulate behaviour in civilised society. To achieve this goal, crimes which shocked the consciousness of humanity, crimes against us all cannot be permitted to go unpunished. I bring these accused before Your Honours to face the charges against them. I do so on behalf of the international community and in the name of all the Member States of the United Nations, and as with all accused in this Tribunal they are brought before you to be tried for their individual criminal responsibility. No state, no nationality, no organisation is on trial for these crimes. Crimes are committed by individual people, and individual people must be held responsible for their criminal acts. There is no such thing as collective guilt before this Tribunal. The case against these accused will be difficult and will take time. The very number of accused in this case will invariably result in challenges for the Prosecution, Your Honours, and the Defence. However, I know that each of the accused will receive a fair trial in accordance with the highest standard of international justice. There can be no justice without the utmost respect for the rights of the accused, and I'm certain that this trial will reflect the absolute commitment of the Office of the Prosecutor to upholding the rights of the accused as well as those of the victims and witnesses. As I said earlier, the surviving victims of the Srebrenica crimes yearn for justice, not vengeance. They look towards this Tribunal to provide justice, to prove the truth of what happened to them and to convict the guilty. This trial is an important step towards and a cause for hope. However, at the commencement of this trial, we must also acknowledge with regret that the effort to bring to justice the most responsible for the terrible crimes in the former Yugoslavia, including the darkest chapter, the genocide in Srebrenica, is incomplete. Unfortunately, two men who should be sitting as accused before Your Honours right now in this courtroom are still at large. I refer, of course, to Ratko Mladic and Zdravko Tolimir. It is absolutely scandalous that these men, along with Radovan Karadzic, have not been arrested and delivered to the Tribunal to face the charges brought against them. The government of the Republic of Serbia is fully capable of arresting these men. It has simply until now refused to do so. Tolimir was, as you know, indicted and joined to the accused in the case before you today. Now, because of the refusal of Serbia to arrest him, his case must be severed from the indictment. Mladic. Mladic should be on trial in this case. It was always hoped and indeed expected that he would be delivered to the Tribunal in time to have his case joined to this trial. Again, the inexcusable refusal to arrest and transfer Mladic means that another Srebrenica trial must be held in the future, when Mladic and Tolimir will be in custody. And make no mistake: He, Mladic, Tolimir, Karadzic, and all the remaining fugitives will be arrested. They will be brought to The Hague and they will be tried for their crimes. This is our pledge to the international community, to the women who mourn for their loss in Potocari, and to all victims of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. Your Honours, Mr. President, I have said what I came before you to say. I have absolute confidence that you will conduct this trial with fairness to all parties and reach a just verdict. With your authorisation, I give the floor now to Senior Trial Attorney Peter McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Del Ponte. Mr. McCloskey. We'll have a break at 10.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, it's a great honour and privilege to be here before you today to give you my opening statement. In 1992, Karadzic and Mladic had a plan for an ethnically pure Bosnian state. For over three years their plan was brutally executed on a massive scale by intimidation, terror -- excuse me. If I could ask the discussion ... This campaign began with the war in the spring of 1992 and continued throughout the conflict, culminating of the removal of the Muslim population from Eastern Bosnia in July 1995 and the Srebrenica genocide. Karadzic and Mladic replied upon a few close associates and political and military system perverted to carry out their war against the Muslim and Croatian armies and the Muslim and Croatian people of Bosnia. I'm not suggesting that the conduct of the entire war was criminal, but in Eastern Bosnia and elsewhere each of the major military endeavours had two objectives. First, beat the enemy. Fair enough. That's war. Second, move out the Muslim population. That is the crime that brought us here. The officers involved cannot separate themselves from this simple truth. To get the job done, Mladic replied upon Generals Milovanovic, Miletic, Gvero, and Tolimir. There were other generals in his Main Staff but none of them were as close to Mladic and therefore not as powerful as these four men. The Main Staff knew the horrors of forcing a people to leave their homeland and yet they all did their part to achieve it. It is unthinkable that in July 1995 any general in the Main Staff had not become fully involved in Mladic's campaign to remove the Muslim population from Eastern Bosnia. The facts of this case will make this abundantly clear. In 1995, General Mladic and his Main Staff looked to their corps and brigade commanders to command the troops in defeating the enemy and removing the Muslim population from their homes. For the Srebrenica genocide and the movement of the Muslim population, General Mladic and his Main Staff replied principally on General Krstic. As you are aware, General Krstic stands convicted by this court of aiding and abetting genocide. In turn, the Main Staff and General Krstic replied upon Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, Vidoje Blagojevic, Major Dragan Obrenovic, Ljubomir Borovcanin and other commanders to defeat the Muslim forces, remove the Muslim population - I'll slow down - and murder the able-bodied men of Srebrenica. Major Obrenovic has pled guilty in this court for doing just that. Main Staff units, such as the 10th Sabotage Detachment, assisted in this awful process. 10th Sabotage soldier Drazen Erdemovic has pled guilty to his involvement in these crimes. The majority of the work in supervising, organising, coordinating, and facilitating the actual removal of the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa and the murder of the able-bodied men from Srebrenica fell to the security officers. For the Main Staff, Ljubisa Beara. For the command of the Drina Corps, Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic. For the command of the Bratunac Brigade, Captain Momir Nikolic. For the command of the Zvornik Brigade, Lieutenant Drago Nikolic and his associate and assistant Milorad Trbic. Momir Nikolic has pled guilty to these crimes. For Zepa, General Tolimir himself was assigned by Mladic to present and be involved in the attack and the removal of its Muslim population. He was assisted in this briefly by Gvero, Pandurevic and security officers Beara and Popovic and others. We will begin the Prosecution by bringing into court a few of the amazing men and boys that survived the mass executions. Without them, the heart of this story cannot be told. We'll move on to the former chief of the Srebrenica investigation, Jean-Rene Ruez, then to the Dutch Battalion soldiers, experts, Bosnian Serb witnesses, and actual video footage, and finally ending with a discussion of the guts of this case the [indiscernible] of this case. None of us will be left untouched by this trial. It will likely be the most important case we will ever try. But the focus of the Prosecution will not be the events and the crime base. These crimes are etched into the terrible history of the Bosnian war. The crimes have never been in serious dispute. We will therefore focus this case on the evidence linking these accused to these crimes. The linkage evidence will come largely from three main sources. The first being documents. Most criminal orders in wartime are given orally, and most of the important relevant military and MUP documents have been destroyed or hidden. However, there are some crucial VRS and MUP documents that will help expose this crime and each of the accused in this court room. Number two, intercepts. You will also see the text of radio intercepts taken down by the Muslim army as they eavesdropped on the VRS and MUP conversations. You will hear all about the process used by the BiH army and I'm confident you'll find this evidence reliable and credible, and they should form an important part of your judgement. Now, you will not be hearing audio of these conversations. Audio does not exist for the vast majority of them. What you will see are transcripts, and you'll hear about the process where the Muslim operators listened carefully to conversations, and when they heard a conversation they started taping it and they would usually get it right in the beginning. They would tape several conversations like this, go to a side room, and carefully transcribe that tape and listen to it over and over again until they had the transcription written down. Then that want saved in handwritten notebooks and then sent out over their intelligence e-mail network and saved in transcripts. And the tapes were used over and over again. They didn't have enough tapes. This will be evidence that will be very important for this case. And of course testimony. Now, some over -- 10 years after these events, there's many more people, many more Serbs that are willing to talk about the events, and many of the VRS and MUP witnesses will directly implicate one or more of the accused with the crime. As you see at the end of our witness list, long lists of VRS and MUP people. Each of these are on that list because they go to the acts or conduct of the accused. But a word of caution here. Many of these witnesses will be adverse witnesses. Many of these witnesses will not be telling you the full truth. Many of the witnesses will go back and forth. However, with your knowledge of the case and your experience, I'm confident that you will be able to glean the truth from these witnesses. And in fact, even in lies you can find the truth. Let me give you one example. You'll be hearing from one MUP supervisor under the command of Mr. Borovcanin. He will acknowledge that he was in Potocari. He will acknowledge he was under the command of Borovcanin. He will lay out the command structure and largely the locations of where his troops were situated. This is extremely valuable information for all of us. Yet at the same time he will actually look at you from this chair and say that he never saw anybody separated in Potocari, even though he was there for two days. Now, I think there is something to be had from this witness even though he is a bold-faced liar and I think we glean something from his bold-faced lie. Why can't he tell about the separations? Simple: It was a crime. All right. I want to talk a little bit about the charges. Despite a massive indictment that got bigger and bigger, I tried to break the basic indictment down into basically it's the two horrendous crimes that the Prosecutor mentioned, the forced movement of the Muslim population and the misery and death resulting from that, and two, the mass murder of the thousands of Bosnia Muslim men and boys. Put those two together and you get genocide. Now, it's important to point out and something that you know but that is a continuing theme with the witnesses especially, is that forced movement is not just about moving the people out, that when done with the knowledge that this is the eventual aim, it involves, one, strangling the enclaves by limiting the crucial supplies; two, terrorising the civilian population by sniping and shelling; three, attacking the civilian population during the assault on the enclaves; and four, moving them out on buses and trucks, or scaring them out by foot, boat, and as you will see, wheelbarrows attached to logs. Substantial involvement in any one or combination of these with the knowledge of the overall plan to remove the population in our view makes an accused criminally responsible. In addition, as set out clearly in the indictment, substantial involvement in an otherwise legal act with the knowledge that such action substantially assists the criminal objective and the intent to do so also makes an accused criminally liable. This is especially true at the high level we're talking about, Generals Gvero and Miletic. For example, when Gvero and Miletic, as part of the overall plan to remove the Muslim population, take part in defeating UNPROFOR with the aim to getting at the population, that makes them guilty because they're part -- It's an overall part and an integral, connected link to the overall criminal objective. Now, the attack on the enclave may not have to be completely illegal, as we'll get into later. Clearly the Muslims were creating a situation that would have allowed the Serbs to attack them and attack the Muslim army. But that does not justify an attack directed towards civilian targets with the overall additional objective to move out the Muslim population. Mass murder. It's crucial to understand that genocide and mass murder is much more than just an order from Karadzic and Mladic and then the people on the ground shooting. This is something that I'm sure the Judges understand, but you'll see from the witnesses that they pretend they don't in many respects. When committed with the knowledge that victims would be killed, the commission of mass murder involves all of the following in equal measure, I'm talking about mass murder as developed in Europe at the end of this century. It involves this: Capturing the Muslim men, detaining the men, transporting the men to detention sites, detaining the men in pre-execution detention sites, transporting the men to the execution sites, executing the men, and disposing of the men. This is the crime of mass murder. We're all familiar with the crime of drugs and the crime of bank robbery and the other crimes and we know how those work, but when someone takes part in any of these activities knowing it's leading to the death and the murder of people, especially at the officer level, they are part of the programme. Any person substantially participating in any of these activities must be found responsible. As a member of a joint criminal enterprise intending the outcome is one way, or as an aider and abettor who has knowledge of the crime and substantially assists in its commission. To drive home the point that these crimes are not just about shooters and Mladic or Karadzic or Milosevic, I want to read you the testimony of a young survivor from the Petkovci dam executions. Witness O from the Krstic trial. He's also a young kid. Remember the Prosecutor's quote of the imam. This guy pulled himself out of beneath some thousand people, 500 to a thousand people, and along with a colleague, even though wounded, managed to survive in the woods and escaped. And when he testified in the Krstic trial, this is what he said: "From all of whatever I have said and what I saw, I could come to the conclusion that this was extremely well organised. It was systematic killing and that the organisers of that do not deserve to be at liberty. And if I had the right and the courage in the name of all those innocents and all those victims, I would forgive the actual perpetrators of the executions, because they were misled." Witness O's organisers, they're in court today with us. That's the focus of this Tribunal. That's the focus of this case. In order to understand Srebrenica and identify those responsible for the crimes, I've always divided this case into roughly three chapters, and I will spend the next few hours going over those chapters with you. The first chapter I call the history leading up to the attack on Srebrenica. It's important to understand the big picture, the historical background, the people, the places, and the events leading up to the attack on the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves in July 1995. And as part of the first chapter, I think we need to have a basic understanding of the make-up and organisation of the army and police forces involved. I'm not going to spend a lot of detail on that. I would refer you when we get there to the reports of Rick Butler and the various officers as they testify, the VRS officers included, but I'll go over a few of the -- what I think are the important issues that you should bear in mind from the beginning of the case. Chapter 2, the fall in Srebrenica and Zepa. These are the events largely from 10 July through roughly 19 July where the population is moved out and the men and boys were killed. Then chapter 3 is what I call direct linkage, and in that chapter I will take documents and intercepts and some discussion of witnesses but not many and discuss each of the accused and show you those documents that when they finally do come into this case will point at each of the accused and implicate the accused in a significant way, and I will go over those with you at the end of my opening statement. I notice we have a break in five minutes. Before we get into chapter 1, might it be a good idea to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Now would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's perfect. So we'll have 20 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. The next break will be scheduled for 12.30. Of course, you're free to ask to have the break earlier or a little bit later, should you -- should it be more convenient for you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I will now get into the -- sort of the briefest history to the lead-up of the events that are in question, and I think it's first important for us to just take a look at the map of Bosnia, and that is -- should be on the screen right now. As you can see, the area within the green is the BiH -- sorry, this is a little fuzzy on my picture, but -- and it's important to note Serbia off to the right of the screen, and the area in the pink is the Drina Corps zone of responsibility where these events largely occurred. It's important to see this area of -- I've referred to as Eastern Bosnia. It's also referred to as the Podrinje area or the Drina River valley, but it's an important area. If you could keep that screen up for me. It's an important strategic area for all sides. If we could get -- did the screen go off on everyone's or just mine? Well, in any event, the show must go on, so I'll continue. In the spring of 1992, the tensions inside and outside Bosnia are pretty extreme. The sides are beginning to form, and this particular area is of important strategic value. And to get an idea of its importance, both strategically and from an ethnic point of view, as this first and foremost unfortunately began as an ethnic conflict, I want to go to an exhibit from the 12th May, 1992, Bosnian Serb Assembly, called the six strategic objectives and talk about them a bit. These -- at this Assembly hearing matters were discussed about moving populations and ethnic populations. And you can see from these -- this directive the ominous tone that this war would take. And if we could blow it up to especially so we can see strategic number 1. And that is, and I'll read it slowly: "Establish State borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities." Now, this is an outrageous thing, to actually attempt to separate ethnic communities, and we'll see just how difficult that was. But they're right up front in this document, and they talk about it. So we see very early on that this war was going to be a war with ethnic motivations relying on old ethnic hatreds and fermenting them. Now, look at number 3. It gives you an idea of how important this area was: "Establish a corridor in the Drina River valley, that is, eliminate the Drina as a border separating Serbian States." Now, you saw the Drina River in the previous map. It was bordering on the Podrinje or Drina River valley and so this would separate that and make this part a part of Mother Serbia, indicating the strategic nature of this area. Now, to give you an idea of the ethnic make-up and the ethnic foundation of this conflict, I want to quote you General Mladic's comments very briefly that he made at this Assembly hearing that led to the promulgation of the six strategic objectives. He says, and this is after having some experience in the war of 1991 in Croatia: "People and peoples are not pawns, nor are they keys in one's pocket that can be shifted from here to there. It is something easily said but difficult to achieve." And he goes on in another part: "Therefore, we cannot cleanse nor can we have an sieve to sift so that only Serbs would stay or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest leave." Then he goes on and says: "I don't know how Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide." General Mladic, of all people, forecasting the event but recognising that moving people from their homeland, Bosnian people from the villages that they've lived in for centuries, was not going to be easy, was going to involve bloodshed. Shortly after this meeting the war in Bosnia, especially in Eastern Bosnia, broke out in earnest. It began in the north in the area of Bijeljina, worked its way south through Zvornik, Bratunac. These events in the spring of 1992 were events notable for their terror and their attacks on civilian population. There were troops from Serbia, paramilitary and others, that were involved in this. Not only were the Muslim forces routed, but the civilians who largely outnumbered the Serbs were shoved and pushed from their homes ever-south, down towards the area of Srebrenica. Now, the BiH in the early days fought back, led by Naser Oric and his own particular brand of horror managed to make some inroads against the -- the VRS. And in -- in November of 1992, Mladic, Karadzic made what I refer to as a supreme act of arrogance and impunity and set out the plan to deal with the Muslims in Eastern Bosnia. And if we could go now to operational directive 4 of November 1992. And in particular, I'd like to -- to blow up section D, page 5 of the English. And as we're doing that, I'll read it to you. There were some nine directives done by Mladic and Karadzic throughout the wartime period. They were important documents. They were sent out to all the corps to outline their objectives, their strategies, and provide them the basic tasks by which they were to work. And if we go to page 5 here and look to the Drina Corps section, I will read the appropriate -- the relevant part. "The Drina Corps: From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad (the dam) Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him and force him to leave Birac, Zepa, and the Gorazde areas ..." Now, that's war. That's fine. That's what war is all about; inflict the heaviest losses possible on the enemy and drive them out. But listen to this last sentence after they want to inflict the losses on the enemy: " ... force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." There it is, black and white, what Mladic had predicted in a secret document. It's called what we now refer to as ethnic cleansing. Move out the Muslim population. In black and white, there it is. Unbelievable. Impunity. Now, as we know from historical fact, the VRS came fighting back, the Muslims forces were being beaten back, and in the spring of 1993 all was practically lost for the Muslims. They had been herded down in the area of Srebrenica, Zepa, and right as the VRS was coming in to make their final attack, General Morillon stepped in with the United Nations and somehow stopped the onslaught and the enclaves were created, for better or for worse. Now, the enclaves were supposed to be demilitarised. They never really were. The meager UN forces that were sent there tried. They were able to get, I think, a tank, the only tank that was known to have, some of the heavier weapons, but the army, the structure remained intact inside the enclave. They had some automatic weapons, a lot of hunting rifles, and they were able to hold a ragtag military force together that led attacks outside the enclave. And so for the next two years we have this situation where from the Muslim side, Naser Oric and the BiH army, are attacking outside the enclave largely in order to tie down troops from other areas of the war and in part defeat themselves, because for the Serb's side of it they were cutting off the enclaves and restricting their humanitarian support. In the early years of this -- we're not going to spend a lot of time in the case but you will hear from one or two Canadian Battalion members to talk about this. But this is not where your indictment starts, but it's important to have some understanding of that. By the time we get to July 1995, we actually see a Muslim document establishing the policy for the BiH army to attack the Serbs out of the enclave in order to tie down the Serbs from going to the Sarajevo front, which in 1995 was the major front for the Serbs, and that's precisely what the BiH was doing. So there was some justification to go into Srebrenica by the Serb army and take out this threat. We'll look at that a little bit later. However, when we look at it in the overall objective, the motive to move out the civilian population, it's a two-part plan, one that may have some legitimacy, and the other that absolutely does not. Now, I'd like to take you to another exhibit to take us a little more into July 1994. It's a report to the members of the Bratunac Brigade, which is stationed right to the north of the enclave, and it basically sets out the strategy on dealing with the enclaves. Now, remember, and we'll get into this in more detail, but you have the Main Staff, the corps, and the brigades. When you see a strategy like this from a brigade, it is not -- it's not coming out of the origin of the brigade commander's head. This is the kind of thing that he will receive direction from above, and he will pass it down to his troops below. But in any event, the brigade that had most of the responsibility for Srebrenica, and if we could go to page 3, it's the last paragraph in paragraph 2 in the English, and as we get there I'll read it. If we can blow it up so we can -- especially with eyes that are not as young as they used to be, if we could blow it up a little more. But the relevant part says: "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave, we must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Again, we see the policy set out that will eventually lead to the attack on the enclaves and gives us a foundation of why we see the sniping and the shelling and the restriction of the material, all of which is happening now but will happen when our case starts as well in March of 1995. Okay. If we leave 1994 and we get into March of 1995, specifically the 17th of March, I think at this point all sides can see that the war won't be lasting forever, and if gains are going to be made they best be made this year. The Croatians were looking to the Bosnian Serb Krajina, and this was the major threat that everyone saw coming as a massive Croatian front to the north. This is where General Milovanovic was assigned for a good part of the year. So General Milovanovic is not present during much of the time and, therefore, not on our radar screen, although he is a very important figure in all of this. He was Mladic's top guy, and when Mladic had a most serious threat, he sent Milovanovic there. He did that with his other generals too. He would send Gvero to Srebrenica to the forward command post. He sent Tolimir the Zepa forward command post. This is how he commanded. Milovanovic was way off in the Krajina during most of this, leaving General Miletic to be standing in for the Chief of Staff. In any event, by this time the Bosnian Serb Supreme Command and military understood that it's now time to solve the issue with the enclaves. If they were going to make them all Serbian, now is the time to do it. So if we could go to operational directive 7 dated 17 March 1995. Okay. And on that I'd like to go again to the Drina Corps section. And by the way, as you'll see at the end of this document, it was drafted by then Colonel Miletic, accused in this case. I'll get into that in a little more detail later when I get to some of the documents associated with General Miletic in particular. But the part I want to particularly note to you in the middle of the paragraph under the Drina Corps, it states: "... while in the direction of Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves." Well, this is military. Zepa and the Srebrenica enclaves were militarily supporting each other. Items were being flown in in secret helicopter missions from the BiH army and creating havoc within the ranks of the villages outside the enclaves and causing the VRS to tie down hundreds of troops around those enclaves away from the Sarajevo front, which was a crucial front. So this part of it is military and is legitimate. "By planned and well thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Again, we're going directly to the civilian population. The inhabitants. There can be no doubt what this means. Again, it's a follow-up on what we see throughout the historical period that I've been mentioning. Right there in black and white, drafted by General Miletic himself. Now, that gets us to where our indictment begins, but before I get to those events, there's a few issues, military issues mostly, that I'd like to discuss that I think you need to have in mind as you look at the case. I would first tell you that by 1995 the VRS was a professional army. It was based on the rules and regulations of the JNA, which was one of the best armies and most professional armies in eastern Europe. It had clear foundations from the Geneva Conventions, the training its officers received by all accounts in my review of it was excellent. Mr. Pandurevic -- excuse me, General Pandurevic was trained in the Geneva Conventions, as were the other professional officers in this group. They knew the difference between right and wrong. They knew what they were doing. These rules of the former JNA were promulgated by the VRS early on, and you can see those rules in Mr. Butler's report. They clearly set out the Geneva Conventions. They actually anticipate an international Tribunal and show respect towards that. They had some good lawyers in the early days of the Main Staff. Unfortunately, that material, that foundation of the honour of the Serb soldier, was never followed, was cast aside. Once they took on the cloak of ethnic war, those that chose to take part of it set aside their honour and began a war against the populations of the Muslims. Now, they had a military prosecutor back then as well, and they promulgated guidelines for determining the criteria of criminal Prosecution. If we could go to that. This is dated 1992, and the part I want to show you in English is on page 7, the third paragraph down, and I'll read it slowly. I think it's that important. It's under a paragraph entitled "criminal offences against humanitarian and international law pursuant chapter 16 of the Criminal Code." "Crimes against humanity and international law can be committed by individuals acting on their own, but by their nature these criminal offences are usually committed in an organised fashion in the implementation of the policy of the ruling circumstances." Witness O's organisers. "Most of these criminal offences are committed only during armed conflicts or are in some way closely connected with armed conflicts, which means that they are committed within the context of the broad military operations and on orders from superior officers." There's no way I could have or anyone else could have said it any better. And this is coming from the Main Staff. They go on to talk about the responsibility of a soldier, especially those of commanders, and I go to the top of page 8. "From this follows the explicit responsibility of the officer corps of the army of Republika Srpska as the giver of orders in command of the armed forces whose members could commit or are committing some of these offences, to take uncompromising action and prevent such conduct. This responsibility belongs by its nature particularly to high-ranking individuals and officials in State military or public organisations or in the concrete circumstances in a position to issue orders." These are commanders. Commanders are the only ones that actually issue or originate orders. In this case, General Vinko Pandurevic, Deputy Commander Ljubomir Borovcanin. I'll talk about the powers and ability to pass on orders and originate orders of the others soon. And I will go on with this quote. "If officers merely find out that units of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska or their members have committed or are committing such acts and take no measures to prevent the consequences or the acts themselves and expose perpetrators to criminal prosecution, this in itself makes them answerable for these criminal offences." They don't prevent it, they're responsible for those criminal offences. Does that sound familiar? Article 7(3). But this is much more than a failure to prevent case, and you'll see this from the facts. When Vinko Pandurevic arrives back to his brigade in the middle of the day on 15 July, there's still some 1.500 people left to murder. And when he comes back, he again is the man in charge on the ground in total command. The people of the Zvornik Brigade are acting under his command when he returns. Ljubisa Beara is there, but he is not a commander. He has no power to command. He is who I've referred to before as an empty vessel. He is only as good as he is filled up by the orders of General Mladic, which he was, and he's carrying them out. He and the other security officers have to get their authority through their commander to obtain the troops and the other machinery necessary to get this job done. But when Vinko Pandurevic returns, he takes on command. He takes on the responsibility of what he absolutely knows is going on, and he knows it. The same holds true with Ljubomir Borovcanin, who has told us in a statement to the ICTY that he was present at Kravica when the massacres were going on and he did nothing. He took a man with burned hands --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really hate to interrupt my learned colleague in giving his opening statement, but we intend to object to the admittance of Mr. Borovcanin's interview, and I believe it would be unfair to quote this in the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, and we will deal with the objection if and when it arises. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin told the ICTY that he was at the Kravica warehouse while the massacres were going on, and he did nothing but take one of his officers who had burned hands to Bratunac. After that, some 500 to 800, maybe more, men were murdered, and his group, his troops were in control of that area and taking part in those murders. Much more than a failure to prevent. You have seen that we have charged in this indictment under a law that requires a commander in an area that he controls to protect prisoners of war, not just his own troops but from anyone that will do them harm. He failed in his duty to do that. Therefore, he's criminally liable. He's also part of the overall joint criminal enterprise and knew that this was a mass murder that was part of an organised plan. You'll see his discussions with Krstic after this fact. You'll see other massacres that his troops were in. You'll see what his troops were doing in Potocari. But I bring this particular section up because it's so important to these two commanders, directly to them. There's another significant rule that was promulgated by Karadzic which had much more importance than the rule I just mentioned. It's entitled "the interim provisions on the service of the army of the Serb Republic, 18 August 1992." And it says: "Members the army shall carry out orders of their superior without demure, in full, accurately, and punctually." This is what went out on the day. As I will discuss later on, General Pandurevic and the rest had received training that they had absolutely no obligation to follow criminal orders. In fact, it was a direct violation of their duty, their honour as soldiers to follow such orders. They knew what they were to do. They were to stand down. All right. Now, if we could talk very briefly about the basic command structure and if I could go to the exhibit chart for the Main Staff. Again, I don't want to get into details at this time. I leave that to the reports of Mr. Butler. And if you could try to blow that up so that we see the top half of it. Sorry, it -- we're left in the electronic age and -- basically this is a chart that puts Ratko Mladic as the commander of the VRS on the top. General Milovanovic is his Chief of Staff. Now, he is the person that is in charge with coordinating the other areas of the command and making sure that the orders of General Mladic get carried out and acting as General Mladic's main advisor. He's Mladic's right-hand man. He's not a commander, but he's close to it and I'll explain how that works. The next boxes under the sheet, first of all on the right are the assistant commanders. Now, assistant commanders are high-ranking officers that are experts in particular fields. For example, the -- well, the fields we're talking about, Tolimir is intelligence and security. Gvero, legal, religious and moral. And there are others. Logistics. And then there are the staff officers who are the staff of the Chief of Staff, and there's various branches within that. In particular, we have the operations department where during most of this time we had Colonel Miletic and then General Miletic as the Chief of Operations. This job also held the position of a deputy Chief of Staff, and so in the absence of Milovanovic, Miletic would take over. And as I mentioned, Milovanovic was in the Krajina for a good part of this, and so the documents that we see throughout 1995 are largely in the hand of General Miletic, who is standing in for the Chief of Staff. Now, as I said, assistant commanders are experts in the field. What they do is they make proposals for the commander regarding their various fields. The commander reviews those proposals, makes his own orders based on them, and then it's the job of the assistant commander to facilitate the commander's orders, make sure they get done. Make sure that it goes down through the chain and gets done. And fundamentally while this is probably a very basic approach to this subject, this is the way it worked in the corps and in the brigade. The fundamental difference is that the Main Staff had very few people and only had a couple of -- of units under arms, the 65th Protection Regiment and the 10th Sabotage Detachment being the ones that are most relevant to this case. Now, an assistant commander may pass on the orders of his commander, or he may issue -- not issue. That's the wrong word. If you say that to a military man, he will grimace. He will make orders that are consistent with his commander's orders originally, and they get passed down through the ranks. He doesn't have the power to originate and issue orders. Therefore, he doesn't have the power to prevent people from committing crimes, because an order to do that that's not backed up. He doesn't have that power. But he passes on the order of his commander, or he makes an order consistent with the order of his commanders, and it has the same effect as if a commander had made it, especially for the soldier or the officer that's receiving it on the other said. And you will see several examples of this happening. Colonel Beara cannot originate orders, but when he wants troops, he has to go, in this case, to General Krstic, asking General Krstic for troops, even though Beara is from the Main Staff. And you'll see this later on. Colonel Beara has to say, but Furtula, another brigade commander is not following the general's orders, namely Mladic. So he's -- Beara has power that is gained through his association and orders provided him by his commander Mladic, and that's the way it works for all these guys down the line. Now, I mentioned briefly about General Miletic and his role. He was the operations -- Chief of Operations. Now, the Chief of Operations is the person that is a hands-on guy involved in the operation, the military operations, of the corps and the brigade. So he is -- he is not a logistician in the other, more technical aspects of it. He is a hands-on guy and connected to these various operations, and so he is a key player in any military organisation. And when he becomes standing in for Milovanovic, I'll try to explain what that means. There is a couple of different designations that the VRS had. They had acting, and they had a -- you could be an acting Chief of Staff, or you could be standing in for the Chief of Staff. Now, the basic difference to this is that when someone becomes an acting Chief of Staff, he's taking on much more of the cloak of that job, and that is in a situation not just in the mere absence or unavailability of the Chief of Staff. It's normally when that Chief of Staff is in the hospital or unavailable or has been dismissed or killed, and this person is standing in -- or excuse me, this person is acting and doesn't have all the aspects of the job itself because it's -- it's assumed to be temporary. But it is much more so than standing in. Standing in is when -- is something that happens in the absence of the person, such as when Milovanovic is still in the army, still in Bosnia, still in communications. He's just far away, engaged up to his eyeballs with the Krajina. So that's the case where Miletic becomes standing in for the Chief of Staff and takes on many of his duties. In fact, almost all of his daily duties. Milovanovic can't do it. You'll see what those are. So that's an important distinction to have in mind as you look at this. Now, commander. It's the same thing but it's a little different in this situation. I'll use the Zvornik Brigade example. In the commander that we see that there is first of all and foremost the commander who is normally present in command, on duty. Then there is the deputy commander who at the same time is the Chief of Staff. Milovanovic was the deputy commander at the same time he was the Chief of Staff. But he only became deputy commander when Mladic was absent or unavailable, which was almost never, even when he was in Serbia. That was not absent. So we don't see Milovanovic becoming deputy commander much. But if we go to the Zvornik Brigade, we see that Vinko Pandurevic frequently goes out on military assignments. His Drina Wolves are the best attack group in the Drina Corps, and he's out on various duties, not infrequently. And we see from the evidence two things happening. Sometimes when he seems like he's gone on a more permanent basis or is fully involved in something well outside the brigade, Dragan Obrenovic has become the acting commander, meaning that he bears almost the entire cloak of command, because Vinko Pandurevic is unavailable to a significant degree. But in other situations such as when we see Vinko Pandurevic go down to take part in the attack on Srebrenica or the attack on Zepa, we see Dragan Obrenovic designated as the deputy commander. This is what he takes on in the absence or the unavailability of the commander. Now, this is an important distinction, because the deputy commander while in command of the troops on the ground and responsible for what's going on in his zone of responsibility, his commander is still in command of him and still has command responsibility. So when Vinko Pandurevic is in Srebrenica, he does not give up his complete responsibility over his brigade. Basically a deputy commander is enough -- is trusted enough, as Obrenovic was, to run the show and do the policies and get the job done as his commander had set the tone. Because this is temporary, that is possible. But the deputy commander is not one to originate policy or originate commands. And if something comes up where the deputy commander must originate or be creative or something outside the -- the area of his command or something he knows his commander did not agree with, he will call his commander and check with him to make sure, and his commander is always available, always had a radio man with him, can get to a post. This war was not fought such that people were pinned down for days at a time out of communication. It gets a little crazier on the 15th and 16th and we'll get into that in detail. But Vinko Pandurevic was always by a radio, always near a forward command post and always reachable. And in the context of his deputy commander, his deputy commander would be contacting him when he had to. That's the basic rules that you'll see. Okay. The security branch. The security branch is just one of the expert branches under each of the -- whether it be the Main Staff, the corps, or the brigade, and the security branch basically has two responsibilities, and it works for each one of them. They have responsibilities associated with law enforcement where they are dealing with -- largely with the military police and enforcing the laws related to military conduct. And practically a lot of this tended to deal with soldiers that left the lines, deserters, and rounding them up and making sure the military police dealt with this properly and that the military police were organised and acting according to the rules. Now, that's part of their job. They were not in command of the military police. The military police were under the command of the commander of the brigade or corps. The security officer was their director and their -- and their supervisor and very clearly established activities related to the military police, and the commanders would allow them to do that with full knowledge of what they were doing. And critical to this case is that military police are in charge of prisoners. So it's very natural that the dealing with the prisoners fell to the military police and the security officers. That's why you see all the security officers sitting here today. They were in charge of dealing with the prisoners. Now, they're not commanders, but they had orders from their commanders, and they're able to give orders pursuant their commanders' orders, and they were able to direct and supervise the military police in carrying out those duties. And that's the way it worked. Now, there's another side of the security branch that you need to be aware of, because they have a two-part job. One, law enforcement. Clearly they have to report everything to their commander. The commander knows what's going on. It's just like any normal situation. The second one is counter-intelligence, and this is unique to this branch. A security officer is responsible for counter-intelligence. Now, what does that mean? In this context, it mostly means threats from within. Internal threats. Threats against the command, threats against the army, soldiers being traitors, soldiers being -- dealing with the other parts of the enemy, espionage. That's counter-intelligence.
