Now, for counter intelligence there are no troops. There is no -- he has no men. It's him basically, the security officer. Sometimes he'll get help from the intelligence officer. They work very closely in matters of intelligence and counter-intelligence. That's why when you -- you'll see that the intelligence officers are very closely related to the security officers and are wrapped up in this thing quite a bit themselves. But -- so one is counter-intelligence, and one is law enforcement. Now, when -- what goes along with the counter-intelligence side are certain privileges that make the security officer's job different than anyone else's, and that is because the security officer has the right to investigate the commander. He can receive information from his other security officers, the ones up the professional chain of command, secretly, and that's -- has been defined in the regulations. He is -- Drago Nikolic is allowed to get secret communications from Popovic or Beara that he can read and Pandurevic cannot read. This drives commanders crazy. It drove Pandurevic crazy, because commanders want to know and be in control of what happens. But naturally when a security officer may be investigating a commander or dealing with very sensitive information that may, if it becomes known to the command staff, infringe upon a -- one of his counter-intelligence jobs, then -- then there's a -- it's obviously a need for some secrecy for that to be carried out. Now, the regulations also clearly say -- they allow that. They understand that, but they say that when it is appropriate, the security officer must tell his commander what's going on. So the security officer may have an operation to ferret out a traitor and he may not have to tell the commander what he's doing, when he's going to go interview that person, but after the interview, when the thing is sorted out he has got to tell his commander what's going on. And he's got to tell his commander he's going there. He can't just go to the front line to interview someone and show up. That would mess up the commanders' ability to run a proper service. So this is a tension that we see throughout -- throughout the VRS. It's a normal tension. Now, as we may see from the Defence, we have seen commanders attempting to blame all the murders on the security branch and suggested that they're running the show, that they're in command. Well, this is impossible in the VRS regulatory scheme of things. There's only, what, four or five security officers for the entire army, and they can't possibly run anything by themselves. They need to rely on the commanders for the men, the material, the troops, all that's involved in this mess. But when we get into this give and take between commanders and security officers, you'll need to have the basic understanding of how the system works. You'll hear that from the witnesses themselves. We'll go through it to the degree that it is necessary. At this point, I can't glean much from the Defence briefs to see if this is necessary. In the past it's been an important topic. As I mentioned, it's the job of the security officer to help direct and supervise the military police. In this case, the -- under the Main Staff, this unit of armed men, the 65th Protection Regiment, designed to protect Main Staff assets had a military police contingent to it and, as such, Beara had a responsibility over them. Not command responsibility but supervisory responsibility. However, going back to the practical aspect of this, you'll see a Dutch soldier, Egbers, who was in Nova Kasaba on the 13th or 14th and was introduced to Mr. -- to Colonel Beara by the commander of the military police unit there in Nova Kasaba, and the commander Malonic introduced Beara as -- here is my commander, Colonel Beara. Now, that's not technically correct, but from Malonic's point of view, Beara -- what Beara said went, and you'll see that in practice. Popovic. There was a Drina Corps military police unit that he directed, and the brigades generally got to know Popovic because he's not far away in Vlasenica and he made visits to the brigades so the brigade military police commanders knew him and of course listened to him when he was working with their security officers. In the case of Zvornik, Lieutenant Drago Nikolic had the Zvornik Brigade military police company that he directed, and in Bratunac we had Captain Momir Nikolic directing the military police company of the Bratunac -- excuse me, platoon of the Bratunac Brigade. Platoon meaning it's a smaller number of men. I believe in the area of 50. Company was supposed to be more in the area of 200. I may have gotten those figures not exact at this point. Okay. Special police. An issue related to the special police that you need to be aware of: The Ministry of Interior is divided -- well, roughly -- it has armed forces, first of all, and their first line of armed forces were the special police, which were divided into regions. And these were some of the top people they originally trained in riot control and that kind of thing. This is where Mr. Borovcanin was as deputy commander. Their units were basically combat units throughout the war that were assigned to work in combat areas, and when they were assigned with the army they came under the command of the army which I'll get into a little bit later. Additionally, the minister of the interior had other combat units related to the police districts that were different than the special police districts. These are the -- basically the civilian police districts, what is referred to as CSBs. Now, the CSB we're talking about is CSB Zvornik which included most of this broad area that we're talking about. And the CSB Zvornik had many, many civilian police officers, traffic officers, detectives, of course, and in time of war it was only natural that those men were used as needed. So they had divided up the CSB into six potential companies. These were call-up companies. They were not always on the front line, but they usually were doing their job, doing traffic control or whatever, but in certain situations they would get called up and used by the army or the Ministry of Interior. And these units we call the PJP units. So we have Borovcanin's special police units and the CSB PJP units. Now, the reason we use this -- these initials PJP is very important, actually, which is why I bring it up. The word in Bosnian that represents the letter P is translated in English as special, and so you'll see many documents with the "special police" of the CSB, and then you'll see "special police" of the Ministry of the Interior, and it can get confusing, so -- and that's just a problem of translation. In Bosnian, "special police," the word is something and, forgive me, but something like "specijal." It sounds like "special." The word that starts with a P, I've forgotten it, but it's different, and so this distinction has to be made. It will drive the members of the MUP as they're on the stand crazy if we mix this up. So we have to use those initials PJP for the municipal police, and we use special police for the special police. Sorry for that long instruction, but with these witnesses it's very important. They obviously take it very seriously, as I know Mr. Borovcanin does. Now, another important area related to this is when the special police, or the PJP units, are assigned to a combat operation that the army is in, the government of the Republika Srpska recognised that this created a problem of command, and so early on they designated special rules that when this happened that you had to get the approval of the minister of the interior and president, and once that happened then the MUP officers and MUP soldiers came under the command of the army that they were assigned to. Now, how did this work? This rule especially points this out so when Borovcanin is assigned by the minister of the interior to go to General Krstic and report to him in Bratunac on the 11th of July, he becomes under the command of the army. Now, I don't have the president's approval of that, but we do have the evidence to show you that that's what's happened. And the way that works is Borovcanin takes his orders from the army, but the rules also clearly set out that the command -- the MUP commanders retain command and their command chain stays the same. So you don't have an army guy going behind Borovcanin's back and giving an order. The rules are Borovcanin gives the orders, they go down through his chain of command, he receives them through the army. Now, of course in the practical battle-field, things don't always work the way it's planned, but that's the way the rules work. That's the way they tried to make them work, and that's the way they did work. It feels like you've been listening to me for a long time and this information is not the easiest to listen to. I now -- it's time to go into chapter 2. I don't know if you want me to keep talking or make a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. McCloskey. We're certainly not going to stop you. I previously told you that the next break was scheduled for 12.30. In reality, I think if we are to stick to the hour and a half schedule, it should be at 12.15 or thereabouts. So please regulate yourself accordingly. I mean, I according to your exigencies. Whenever you need to stop, I will give you the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a natural stopping point, and I don't think people should have to listen to me for more than 45 minutes at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we'll have a 20-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I know that first 37, 38 minutes of today's sitting was dedicated to something else, so you had 38 minutes less. Do you think you would be able to finish your opening statement today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. As I look at it, and as I realise the pace I'm going, I don't think so. I would like, if possible, to have at least a couple of hours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And can I then kindly ask you to stop ten minutes before the scheduled time of -- of 13.45 so that we'll deal -- we'll have some oral submissions on the outstanding motion on protective measures so that we'll then proceed to decide that either later on today or earlier -- or later on tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, as I've stated, chapter 2, entitled "the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, by May and June of 1995," the VRS had finally been able to engage itself to focus on the enclaves, and they developed an attack plan to do just that, and it lays out the attack and the purpose of the attack, and I would like to go to that plan to just show you one part of it that is important to what I've been saying in the theme of the case, and that is page 3 of what is entitled "the command of the Drina Corps Military Secret Krivaja 95," and basically lays out the situation, the military situation, and assigns the units that are going to be taking part. And I want to point out to you on page 3, the third paragraph from the top. If we could go to that in English. And I'll read it slowly.: "The Command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to Operations Directive no. 7 and 7/1 ..." Now, if you recall, directive 7 was the one that said make life unbearable for the inhabitants of Srebrenica. So basically again, and I'll quote: "... pursuant to Operations Directive no. 7 and 7/1 of the VRS Main Staff and on the basis of the situation in the corps area of responsibility, has the task of carrying out offensive activities with three forces deep in the Drina Corps zone, as soon as possible, in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and reduce them to their urban areas." Now, as we've said before, separate the enclaves is a legitimate military concern, but look at this, the last part: "... reduce them to their urban areas." Now, both enclaves are some 50 to 60 kilometres in diameter, and the bulk of the population of Srebrenica, which is some 30.000 - perhaps even more - live outside the roughly 1 kilometre by 2 kilometre urban area. So if you attack that enclave and you reduce it to the urban area, you are forcing some 15, 20.000 people into a tiny area that would create an absolute humanitarian disaster. So it was the purpose of this plan to do just that. Now, if you look at the plan in more detail you'll see that it was not the purpose of the plan to take the enclave at that time. It was the purpose to reduce it to its urban area, to create this horrible situation, and later in this document you'll see it says create a situation for the elimination of the enclave, and something that -- be prepared to act when given the opportunity. Something any good criminal -- sorry, any good military commander would do in the situation. And so it's important to note that while we see directive 7 at work here and we see the unlawful aim, they're not at that point trying to take the enclave. You'll see in other documents what they're worried about is the United Nations and NATO. There are other documents that say when -- when the UN leaves, then take the enclave. So like Morillon in 1993, with the UN there they're worried about their view in the world and not prepared to take it. It wasn't until a little later, as the events unfolded, they became willing to, and we'll get into that. All right. If we could go to -- can you get to the map with the four S's. I'm going to skip to the end now and show you a map that was found in the Drina Corps collection that we have the original of. You won't get the full feel of it for -- on this -- on this screen. In fact, if we could blow it up a bit more so we could try to read the English. This -- this is a map, an actual JNA military map of the Srebrenica enclave in the north - that looks pretty good - and the Zepa enclave in the south. This was a map that was drawn after the operations were over and were signed and stamped as an official military map, as you can see, by Major General Radoslav Krstic. And what is stated on them is interesting. "Srebrenica has been Serbian and remains Serbian." Then it says, "12 July 1995." And then: "Zepa is also Serbian. 27 July 1995." 12 July is the day they entered Potocari and finally took the enclave, and 27 July is the date that they took Zepa. And you can see they've -- they've drawn the basic attack plan, and the red is the Serbs, the blue is the Muslims, and the little initials are for the various brigades that were involved in the attack. You'll see the Zvornik Brigade involved in both, Vinko Pandurevic and the Drina Wolves playing a major role in those. You may also notice, if you look at this map, over the top of this map is written a big cross with four Cyrillic S's in it, and that, as you likely know, is a Serbian national symbol. Nationalist symbol. It's not just a national symbol. Had there been a flag on this map, a Serbian flag, well, that's one thing. This is a -- is a symbol of Serb nationalism, and those S's stand for "Only unity will save the Serbs." Now, this -- this saying "Only unity will save the Serbs," is in itself relatively harmless sounding, but it's based on the propaganda that was used from the very beginning of this war that the Muslims were coming to kill us all. They're coming to commit genocide on us. We must fight for our survival. This is a theme you hear repeatedly in the speeches of General Mladic, General Krstic, and others, and it's the very simple propaganda as a rallying cry to not just fight, but when you believe that the opposite forces are coming to commit genocide on you, that is your first step towards the dark side. And so what do we have here? Skip to the end. Srebrenica. You can see look under that cross, those four S's, and think of the some 7.000 people that are dead and buried under them. A little farther north in Zvornik, to be precise. And in Zepa, the people have been run out and the top leadership murdered. Three, four, at least, people were murdered in Zepa. So we have as an official military map, General Krstic, who has been convicted of aiding and abetting, putting his national symbol over the top of the graves of Srebrenica. They are proud -- he is proud of what he's done. It gives you an idea of the attitude of General Krstic personally. But more than that, because, as you'll see over and over again in this case, the theme that a commander leads by example. When a commander exhibits this kind of nationalistic horror, he is signalling to his troops that it's okay. When Mladic issues orders saying remove the population, he's signalling to his generals and his troops that it's okay. When a commander allows this and sells this and pushes this and acts like this, this is what leads to the kind of tragedy that we had. You'll hear Momir Nikolic. He stood up and testified that he allowed the horror of Potocari to happen in front of him. The kickings under the bus, the beatings, the people being taken off. And he said by his very presence as an officer from the brigade, he contributed to what was going on, and any other officers present that allowed this to happen in front of them contributed to this. This is a very important command concept that I know General Pandurevic has been taught and I know the other people have been taught, and they've seen it happen, and a commander leads by example. The examples set early on were this. Here a classic example: Lead by genocide. Okay. Now, let's chronologically go to the -- to the case itself. Excuse me a minute. We'll get away from the machine for just a second. I don't know if you can all see that. There's not a perfect place to put it. Okay. If we can put it on the chair. Thank you for helping with that. I hope you can get some idea of that. Now, the attack began in earnest on 6th July, and by 9 or 10 July the Muslim forces were beginning to crumble. The UN, who had been the focus of near attacks, they shot in and around the OPs, the posts that were all around the enclave, they started moving back towards their base in Potocari. At one point, I believe it was on the 7th or 8th of July, a Muslim army person got very upset by this and tossed a hand grenade onto a Dutch armoured personnel carrier and killed a Dutch soldier. After that, the Dutch went to the Serb side and were taken by the -- by the VRS in a humanitarian way and set up in the Hotel Fontana. However, they were not allowed to return to their base a few short miles down the road to Potocari. They were held there. And as you'll see from the evidence, they will held there as hostages. So we have hostages on the 8th of July, 9th of July. So by the 9th and 10th of July, the Muslim forces are crumbling. For some reason the BiH forces had taken Naser Oric and his chief people out of the enclave several weeks earlier, and so the people that were there in command tried but got no help from NATO or the UN forces, and so by the 10th of July it looked pretty grim for the people of the enclave. The UN is trying to get NATO airstrikes approved through the UN bureaucracy and that's not happening, and the Muslim army is crumbling under the tough attack of Pandurevic and the other forces. And so if discussion with Radovan Karadzic, Karadzic decides that it's time to -- to take the enclave, that the position is right, that the UN is not putting up any -- any resistance, and if they do, they have hostages. And so what we find the next day, on the 11th of July, is when the NATO actually does come in and as a last-ditch effort to try to bomb the Serb forces, and they do drop a couple of bombs, the NATO -- the command of the Dutch Battalion receives word from the Serb forces that we're going to kill the men -- your men that we have unless that stops. So that stopped. No more NATO Air Force, and the Serbs are free now to roll right in. Now, we see the decision of President Karadzic on July 10th in a document which I'll show you a little later when I get to the specific evidence regarding General Gvero, because it's a letter from Tolimir who is passing on the directions of the president saying it's now time to go in and take the enclave. You'll also see the president ordering that UNPROFOR not be touched and the civilians not be touched and the Geneva Conventions be used. That's on the 10th. Of course, the very next day the Serb authorities threaten to kill all the hostages. But the important part about this letter is that it's directed personally to Generals Krstic and Gvero who -- at the forward command post at Pribicevac. That shows that General Gvero is at the command post with General Krstic who is leading the attack. So this is a very typical Mladic command structure. He's not Milovanovic in the Krajina, he's got Tolimir in the Zepa area, and he's got Gvero at the key point during the key moment of Srebrenica. And so on 11 July, Mladic marches triumphantly through the city of Srebrenica with Vinko Pandurevic, with Krstic, with General Zivanovic who was the then corps commander of the Drina Corps. Popovic is there. You'll see this on video. It's an amazing -- amazing video of what happened. And if we could go to an exhibit. I'll just take a still just give you a bit of flavour of the Mladic looking into the camera that is purposefully being done. He looks into the camera and he says: "Finally, after the rebellion against the Dahis, the time has come to take revenge upon the Turks in this region." This is again a foreshadowing of Mladic's intent, what he has in mind. Now, the rebellion against the Dahis occurred on the 13th of July in 1817 and was an uprising of Serbs against Turkish mercenaries or rulers of some sort. So we have Mladic going back well into history for Serb television giving them this message, which was to foreshadow the events. So on the 10th, the 11th of July, we -- in response to the Serbs making it into the town of Srebrenica after shelling civilian targets, dropping at least several mortars into a crowd of people around the Dutch Battalion, the women and children and some men move towards Potocari, which down here, as you can see, is just a few kilometres north of Srebrenica and was where the main DutchBat compound is. They have a small compound in Srebrenica, but it is, under shelling and pressure from the Serbs, soon dismantled. So by the evening of 11 July, Srebrenica has been taken. Some 20 to 30.000 women and children and military -- and roughly a thousand military-aged men have moved into Potocari. At the same time, about 15.000 mostly military-aged men but some women and children start to move towards the villages of Susnjari and Jaglici on the map as you can see them, and where it has been decided that they are going to make a run for it to go through what has been an established smuggling route towards the territory of the BiH army, which is this grey line, towards the town of Nezuk. Now, this column is hard to estimate, but their best estimate has been about 15.000, about a third of which were armed with automatic weapons or rifles, hunting rifles, with some RPGs, shoulder-fired grenades, and little else. You'll see an amazing video scene of these men assembling, a few with rifles and many without. So they are gathering on the evening of the 11th and late night of the 12th and begin to head across the tough terrain from Jaglici northward. At this point there's nothing really much stopping them but a minefield and a few civilian soldiers in trenches that really aren't prepared to handle that kind of event, and the area they go in is so rough there's not even trenches down there. But the night of the 11th of July, there are two famous meetings between Mladic and the Dutch Battalion command at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac. The Dutch command, of course, was very concerned with the situation, was not allowed to have any outside help from NATO or from -- Morillon was not allowed to come in, or Janvier would have been the person that was present and in charge at the time, and so they were on their own. And You'll see that, and you'll see how frightening this situation was. So Karremans asked for a meeting and they had a meeting, and Mladic at that meeting threatens Karremans, screams at him. You'll see the tape. And then asks for a Muslim representative to come an hour later. The Dutch go get a Muslim representative from the crowd, just a guy that was a teacher, and he comes that night, and Mladic talks with him. Mladic is obsessed with the military. Where are the military? Turn -- you know, the military-aged men demanding their surrender and that everything will be fine. And he looks at this man and you see it, and he says, "It's up to you, sir, whether your people survive or disappear." That's the most frightening genocidal talk imaginable. And then he sets up a meeting for 10.00 the next day where they will organise the transportation of the Muslim population out of Potocari. And so the morning of the 12th the column is -- has started moving out, and at 10.00 they meet again at the Hotel Fontana. But that morning the Serb forces, including Borovcanin's forces, come into Potocari, you'll see this on the video, and take over control of the situation. This is where crimes first start happening, where the soldiers are allowed to take out their vengeance, their whatever on the civilian population. You'll hear evidence of bodies, of assaults. We have tried to put that in -- most of it through 92 bis and other evidence, but it is a -- that's when the horror of Potocari begins. Now, the night of the 11th, Mladic was together with his main commander, General Krstic, also with Zivanovic. He had an intel officer from the Main Staff named Radoslav Jankovic. They were all there together. Popovic was in the area, was at the meeting on the morning of the 12th. It's very clear from the evidence that the plot, the plan to absolutely kill and murder the Muslim men of Potocari was hatched that night, the night of the 11th, the night of the 12th. Now, it was clear from intelligence reports that there was roughly a thousand military-aged men in the town of Potocari. So Mladic knew that on the night of the 11th, and when they -- the army refused to surrender and nothing was going to happen, clearly Mladic made the decision that night that the -- that the men would be separated and killed. You'll see as I discuss, you know, the various evidence that supports that, but that's when the decision was made. You first see it again in a televised -- well, not televised but -- it's a video. Some of it is televised, but a video of portions of that meeting. And one part that was cut out of the video was when Mladic told the assembled people at this meeting, again with the Dutch Battalion, civilian members of the Muslim community, and civilian members of the Bratunac community, Mladic demanded that the able-bodied men 16 to 60 be screened as war criminals. So Mladic had made the decision that night to screen men as war criminals. Okay. Now, shortly after that meeting, buses, trucks arrived, and the first separations in Potocari began in the early afternoon. But what we see is no screening. What's happening is a wholesale separation of anybody from roughly 15 up to 78, as you heard the Prosecutor, and some very young boys and some very old men and everyone. No screening. No names. No interrogations to speak of, nothing that would have been legitimate for them to go in and look for soldiers and take soldiers aside or people suspected of being soldiers and keep them and -- keep them for exchange. What was not legitimate was what they did: A wholesale separation and transport out of the area of the men. So this is the first indication that their intentions are not honourable. They had a lot of intelligence they could have gained, a lot of value in having hundreds of prisoners, because there were hundreds of Serb prisoners in Muslim prisons, and these men could have been exchanged to get their own soldiers back. But instead, wholesale screening, nobody is writing names down, and most importantly, they're not given any food, any medical help. They're put in horrendous conditions where they're jammed in buildings and vehicles, and they're beaten and starved and killed over the two or three days that the men from Potocari were stored there. So when you put all that together and you see this happening on the morning -- or the afternoon of the 12th, the evening of the 12th, 13th, continually it goes on, it's very clear that Mladic, what he had in mind for these men of Potocari, that they were marked for death. There's no question about that when you put all the evidence together. There's a photograph we have of a huge, massive pile of IDs burning on the side of the road in Potocari, I think on the 14th of July. IDs, any documents in any military interest is a key thing to get when interrogating someone so you know who they are, what unit they may be from, that kind of material burned without a care in the world. They had no idea that the international forces of NATO would be visiting them in January of the next year, and the arrogance by which they perpetrated this is amazing. So in the afternoon of 12 July the forcible transfers and murders begin. Just to give you the briefest look of a photo of Potocari so you get a feel for this. You'll see the video. I don't want to take the time to show you the video now, but if we have that photo of the thousands of people in Potocari. I don't recall if this is the 12th or the 13th, but it gives you an idea of just the masses of numbers of people. And in this crowd you will see military-aged men, most of whom are now dead. And if we go to the next photograph of the men separated. There's another still, a photograph. It's hard to tell from this photograph, but these are trucks, and the women are walking on one side of the trucks and the men are walking on the other. They have been separated and directed. And take a look at the men. Look at these old guys. They're not interviewed, they're not interrogated, they're just separated out. And we have -- several of these men have been identified and presumed dead. We will have a booklet of these stills that identify the people that have been killed. But this is the separation, the wholesale screening -- wholesale separation, non-screening, excuse me. I think we have another one of Mr. Borovcanin. Again, this is 13 July of -- and Mr. Borovcanin, whose troops have been in and around Potocari on the 12th and 13th taking part in the separations, this is a United Nations military observer in the forefront, Mr. Kingori from Kenya, and with a Dutch officer, and they're discussing the various events. Kingori is very concerned about what is going on right across the street from where they're standing. I don't know, do we have a picture now of the white house? Right across from where Mr. Borovcanin is standing, and this will be made more clear in the video, is the famous white house where men, after they were separated, were taken. Here is a shot of the balcony of the white house some, I don't know, 40 metres, 30 metres from where Borovcanin was standing, facing this. These are the Muslim men huddled in -- in a mass, looking through the slats of the -- the balcony. All those men are to be killed later down the road; two, three days later. And if they're lucky, they're killed in Bratunac by a soldier with a gun. Now, Momir Nikolic will tell you that he coordinated the separations and the movement of the population out, and he did it with a commander under Mr. Borovcanin's command named Dusko Jevic, known as Stalin. He is the person I spoke of earlier who is pretty good with the organisation and was present in Potocari but didn't see anybody separated. Momir Nikolic will also tell you that on the morning of 12 July, after the morning meeting at the Hotel Fontana, Vujadin Popovic and the Drina Corps intelligence officer, Mr. Kosoric, came up to him and said that the decision would be -- has been made to separate the military-aged men and kill them, and we need you to help organise this and help get the job done, and they ask him for locations to kill people. He provides them with the locations of something called the brick factory, which you may soon see. It's an area on the outskirts of Bratunac a lot like the Kravica warehouse, perfect for storing people to be killed. And then Momir Nikolic acknowledges that he took part in the separation and the movement of the women and children and the men, knowing that the men were all going to be killed. Okay. On the 12th of July, in the evening, there is a meeting with General Mladic, General Krstic, and the brigade commanders. After Srebrenica fell on the 11th, most of the brigade commanders involved in the assault stood down briefly. They weren't exactly where the forces of Naser Oric were. They thought they were in the area called the Bandera Triangle south of the enclave. But on the 12th Mladic called a meeting of all the commanders. And it's important to note that at this point the murder operation has been decided. There are probably 500 to a thousand Muslim men separated and jammed into vehicles and schools at the Vuk Karadzic school complex in Bratunac, and they're beginning to be preyed upon; beaten, killed by their captors. So just down the road from that is the meeting at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, and clear that Vinko Pandurevic is there with General Krstic, General Mladic. There are other brigade commanders; Mirko Trivic, the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, will tell us some of about what happened at that meeting, I'm sure not all, but it's inconceivable that that evening that Mladic and Krstic did not inform Generals Pandurevic and others - Colonel Pandurevic at the time - and others about what was going on and the plan. Now, it's also important to note that at this time there had been no plan to move any prisoners up to Zvornik. All they had and all they really knew about were the thousand men from Potocari, and they were looking to murder them around Bratunac in places that Momir Nikolic had talked about, the brick factory. So -- but given that and the import of that and the fact that they're all together in the command, it's beyond belief that they did not discuss this. But what you will hear about is that now Mladic had made the decision to take on Zepa, and so Mladic tells his commanders at a brief meeting okay, on to Zepa. We've got Srebrenica, on to Zepa. Some of the brigade commanders, Vinko Pandurevic being one of them, stood up to Mladic and said, you know, that his troops were tired, that they needed some rest, and perhaps there were other military reasons that he had, and Mladic insisted, and the brigade commanders were able to convince Mladic to come down to this area of Viogor where the troops were established and give the troops a pep-talk and get them going, which is what he did the next day. Okay. That takes us to the 13th of July. Now, on the 13th of July, we -- remember, we have the column moving out of Jaglici and Susnjari on the night of the 11th, and on the 12th, a significant number of them make it across this road, the Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road. A great flaw in the Serb intelligence is they don't realise at the time that -- how many did. At least 5, 6, 7.000 Muslim men made it across that road early on in this. But at least half the column got stuck back. By the night of the 12th, with the help of Borovcanin's forces and other forces coming in, the Serbs were able to seal off this road from Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and to Kravica, the area where the Muslim column were -- were advancing. So by the morning of the 13th, there was an iron ring on that road, and the -- some 6.000 Muslim men, 5, 6.000 Muslim men were trapped up on the woods behind it, and the Serb forces went up and down that road with megaphones and dressed in UN gear and with UN APCs calling them down to surrender, that they would be safe, that the UN would look out for them, and many did. Five, 6.000 under the Serb numbers on the 13th this happened, and they were assembled at various places, Sandici, Nova Kasaba, and sent to the warehouse in Kravica. Now, it's the morning of the 13th, another watershed date and time to remember, that the organised mass executions really begin. Before that, we've seen isolated acts of brutality and death. Isolated in the context of Srebrenica, that means a hundred people minimum, bodies piling up in the Vuk Karadzic school complex, bodies in the woods in Potocari, but we don't see the kind of organised mass executions that this case is known for. But on the morning of 13 July, 16 men -- Muslims are assembled at the intersection of Konjevic Polje and they're put on a bus and they're taken up to an area just north of that along the river, the Jadar River just about here. We'll get a better map of that so you can see that. And they're taken down to the river and executed. We know that because a man survived that. He was shot through the shoulder, fell into the river, and the river had a pretty good current and it washed him away, and he managed to survive and tell the story, and he's got a bullet hole in his shoulder to prove it. But the important thing about this story is that they took a bus. Now, a bus at this time of day was a crucial item, because they were really trying to get the women and children out of Potocari. So for the military or the MUP to get a bus showed that there is some organisation behind these killings and that killing 16 people and using a bus is not something privates or sergeants are going to do on their own. So that's our first indication that we have an organised mass execution going on. Then a little bit later, maybe 12.00, 1.00, we have a witness that -- that sees three busloads of Muslims go down a little road towards the Cerska valley, right here. He's in -- he's up in the woods looking down, and he sees it followed by an APC with soldiers and then shortly after by an excavator, and he hears all kinds of gunfire and shortly thereafter the buses come back empty and the bulldozer comes back, as does the APC. As he's trying to escape north, he comes across an area that was -- had a horrible smell, and he showed us that area. And back in I believe it was 1998, we excavated that and found 150 Muslim men with their hands tied behind their back with wire ligatures and shell casings all over the road and dirt that had obviously been moved by an excavator just thrown on top of them. So that murder happened about 1.00 p.m. Obviously, again the important part about this murder for our purposes is it had three buses, an APC, and an excavator. Privates, sergeants, they don't do that on their own. This mass execution is happening at this point at the highest channels now. Cerska valley shows it. But what perhaps the VRS didn't understand is the massive amount of prisoners they would get. By the afternoon of 13 July, it's not just 150 men here or 16 men there. They literally have 5 or 6.000 people assembled, and I believe it becomes clear to them they cannot kill all these people in Bratunac, although you will hear testimony that Beara to. He wanted to start doing it and was very angry when they didn't. But on the evening of the 13th of July, most of the prisoners that had been held in Nova Kasaba and Sandici, these big fields, had been transported to Bratunac or the village of Kravica where they were stored. About a thousand of them were put in this Kravica warehouse just outside the little village area, and in the afternoon it was decided that they should be murdered at the -- near the same time that buses were being transported down the road. They parked buses in front of the warehouse and they began killing people. And the killing lasted for hours and hours. There was at least 800 to a thousand people in two sides of this warehouse. I'm going to go into that in more detail with you when I get to Borovcanin, because this is a murder crime that you really need to understand. The warehouse and what the witnesses are saying and what Borovcanin is saying, it's a whole event within a trial itself, and it's -- unlike most of these cases the detail of this event will be important for your consideration. Okay. Now, as I mentioned, there were so many prisoners on the 13th they couldn't kill them all, and they made the decision to move them up to Zvornik. We know this -- well, Momir Nikolic tell us this. In fact, Momir Nikolic says that he goes and sees Drago Nikolic and provides him the information about that. But we also have a survivor from a school in Bratunac who was put in a vehicle along with 50 to a hundred others and shipped up to the Zvornik area the night of the 13th and put in the Orahovac school. Right here. Not far from the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. So we know that on the night of the 13th that they realised that they cannot kill everyone in the Bratunac area. You'll hear a famous intercept between Miroslav Deronjic, the head of the SDS party, and -- and Radovan Karadzic where Karadzic is told of the thousands in the schools and says, "Yes, but get them into warehouses outside, outside," and Deronjic says, "Yes, yes." And Deronjic will testify about that. So on the 13th, the Muslim men are beginning to be sent off to Zvornik. Now, on the 13th, Colonel Pandurevic was sent with his troops to Zepa and was in the Zepa area of operations at the time this decision was made, but he would have been in radio contact and been able to be identified. And this is the kind of thing, as I go back to deputy commander, that he would have been told about. And you'll hear about the evidence that he was told about it. That he's on the radio -- he's available and he's contactable by the radio. But the next day, on the morning of the 14th, the attack begins and his troops are part of that attack. Anyway, back to the evening of the 13th. This is where the Muslims are -- are held at the schools, some few hundred that night, but then for whatever reason, under the darkness or the security situation because the Muslim column is still out there, they stop their transporting that night, and on the morning of the 14th they gather a massive convoy of buses and trucks to load these some 5.000, perhaps 6.000 Muslim men and boys that had been stored in Bratunac and Kravica, the surviving ones, and ship them up to Zvornik. This column is led by Lieutenant Colonel Popovic and the chief of the Bratunac Brigade military police and others. On the afternoon of 14 of July, the organised murders begin at the Orahovac school. Men are taken out of the school building, put on little Zvornik Brigade trucks moved about -- less than a kilometre down the road, unloaded and summarily executed by firing squad, members of the Zvornik Brigade. All of this is done by members of the Zvornik Brigade, and specifically the 4th Battalion are involved. At the same time, there are people that had been moved to the schools at Petkovci, Rocevic, and in the school at Kula in the area of Pilica and the Pilica cultural centre. I will go in some more detail about each of the accused, their whereabouts and their involvement at the end, probably tomorrow. The executions at Petkovci started late night, the 14th, after the executions had finished at Orahovac, went all night, probably 800 to a thousand persons murdered. We don't know who actually pulled the trigger during that. We know that the battalion, I believe it's the 6th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade was involved in transporting people to be killed. And the school was right across the street from the battalion command post, and you'll hear testimony from the battalion commander and deputy commander about Beara being present and organising these prisoners. The next day, on the 15th, Pandurevic has been given an urgent call from Obrenovic. The column is really beginning to threaten Zvornik on the 14th. There's clashes here between the column and the Zvornik Brigade forces. Zvornik Brigade realises that it's not the 2 or 300 that they originally thought. It's more like 5.000 and Obrenovic is getting really panicked. And so on the night of the 14th, he calls for urgent help and asks for Vinko Pandurevic. But I left out a key point. I'm sorry, I want to go back on Obrenovic. As you know, Obrenovic pled guilty, and on the evening of the 13th, Obrenovic will testify that while he's dealing with the column he gets a phone call from Drago Nikolic who has been assigned to be at the Zvornik Brigade forward command post up here in the woods, and roughly what Drago Nikolic tells him is that thousands of prisoners are coming to Zvornik. It's been ordered that they be detained and shot and that he needs to be relieved from his duties at the forward command post to help organise this and facilitate it. Obrenovic says, "Wait a minute. We've got to have authority from our commander on this." And Nikolic says, "It's coming from the top," and he's been contacted and -- by Popovic, I believe, and that it's coming from the top, that the command is coming from the commanders. At that point, Obrenovic, trusting his security officer, and being part of what Obrenovic called the vortex of hatred, relieved Drago Nikolic from his responsibility, authorised him to get military police to begin the job of guarding and receiving these prisoners and killing them and authorised the entire murder operation for that area and pled guilty to that. So -- but getting back to the 14th, he manages to get through to the Drina Corps command, who gets through to Pandurevic. Pandurevic comes back mid-morning, probably around noon on the 15th. Now, when Pandurevic arrives, everyone at Orahovac is dead and the burying process is continuing. That's roughly a thousand people. Everyone from Petkovci is dead and the burying process is happening that day that he's coming back. And this is Zvornik Brigade engineering officers and equipment that are involved in this massive burial process. So when he comes back, everybody from those two schools is dead. Roughly 2.000 people. But there are still at least 1.500 located in Pilica, in the cultural centre, and the school at Kula, and maybe 500, maybe 800 located in the school in Rocevic who are in the process of being killed as he comes back. Obrenovic reports all of this to him, fundamentally that they're having problems guarding and killing -- excuse me, guarding and burying all these people. There's no mention of problems killing them. It's guarding them and burying them is a big problem, and Pandurevic's response to Obrenovic on that point was civil protection was supposed to take care of that. Now, civil protection is the outfit that does sanitation and burials and had taken care of this in Bratunac. So this was an indication to Obrenovic that Pandurevic had been informed and was probably not happy about his units having to take part in this to take them away from their duties and had been informed that civil protection would be doing that. He's not concerned about the deaths of these men. He's concerned about his units and men that would take them away from their military duties. So after Pandurevic gets briefed, Obrenovic has other meetings at the brigade command. He does what a good commander should do and he goes out to the front and leads the -- leads the defence. He initially argued with Obrenovic and the other folks who said, "We need to open this and let these people through, because we're going to lose too many troops in the process." We can't deal with the situation. The situation is thus: The -- the front line is here. BiH troops are here north of Nezuk with artillery, with men in trenches, with other equipment, and you've got some 5, 6.000 partially armed men coming at them from their rear. And on the night of the 15th, Zvornik is in trouble, and initially Pandurevic disagrees and wants to take on this whole -- whole column, but when he gets there there's a huge -- on the morning of the 16th and you'll read about it in the intercepts, and there's a 19th century battle is the only way I can describe it. Just hundreds of, many of them unarmed men, swarming over trenches of the Zvornik Brigade, taking their heavy weapons and turning them on the Zvornik Brigade. By the early morning hours of the 16th, the Zvornik Brigade has lost some 50 people. Now, in this war, 50 people in a morning battle is enormous losses. And it's at that point that Pandurevic re-thinks his decision, and eventually the decision is made to open up an area to allow the rest of the people to go through. That stays open for a couple of days and then it's closed. But it's done not out of humanitarian reasons but because 50 Serb boys were killed because of Mladic's wonderful scheme to take the Srebrenica enclave. So also on the day of the 16th, the executions continue. Popovic is involved and so is Beara in the killings up in Pilica where there's some, I said, about a thousand people at the school, maybe 500 in the cultural centre. You will see the specific evidence that shows their involvement and the 10th Sabotage Detachment that was brought in to help the killing process, but the killing occurred at the Branjevo Military Farm. It's called the Branjevo Military Farm because it was just that. It was a unit of the Zvornik Brigade that raised pigs and grew crops to feed the troops, and it had -- it was lead by an officers and had soldiers working there. And this was made available for this operation, and it was Vinko Pandurevic's unit and Vinko Pandurevic's land, and it was his soldiers that helped make all this happened. They were guarding the people at the school. They were holding down the Branjevo farm. The 10th Sabotage came in to actually do most of the killing and then moved down to the Pilica centre in the afternoon of the 16th to kill off the people at the cultural centre. On the 15th the executions had occurred at a place called Kozluk, just so that sticks in your head. And it's not far from the Rocevic school. Now, after the murders in Pilica on 19th of July, we see many Muslim groups are still caught in the woods and running around and a unit from the Krajina Corps that was sent and resubordinated to Vinko Pandurevic captured a group of people, about -- I think there were 10 of them, and according to the survivor they got on the radio, talked to someone on the radio, and after that everyone was -- except one was shot and killed. Our survivor was shot in the back and rolled down a hill and was able to escape to tell us this. But those men were under the command of Vinko Pandurevic, resubordinated to his brigade. You'll see the order by -- or the directive by General Miletic assigning that Krajina Corps crew to Zvornik to help the -- help the situation, the combat situation that was going on. So you can see from some amazing evidence the linkage between -- between all these people. I'm not going to go into the detail of all the other murders. You will -- you will hear about the murder of some 16 patients that were seriously injured near Milici, down in the south, and were sent to Zvornik hospital, but instead of the ICRC being brought in, these seriously injured people were sent to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters around the 14th, 15th, something like that, and were held in their -- in their area, in their medical area. And you'll hear from the doctors of the -- from the Zvornik hospital came and treated them, and Obrenovic went and looked after them because there was issues related to the soldiers not liking Muslims being in the command. And shortly after this, Popovic arrived and those prisoners were taken out and they've never been seen since. Why they needed to kill 16 people from Milici that were seriously injured patients, I don't know, but they did. We have their names. They're clearly on the missing list. And Mr. Popovic is related to that. We also -- we know from a survivor of the Branjevo farm that he in his escape from under the bodies on the 16th, he finds four other survivors from the Branjevo farm, and he learns about what villages they're from, and he sees the blood on them and hears their story. And then a few days later, they were assisted by a couple of soldiers from the Zvornik Brigade and given a sandwich and told where the front line was. Those guys were farmers. I think they were helping -- helping their family at the time and helped out these four pathetic Muslim guys. Well, those four guys, the Muslims, got captured later on and were interrogated by Drago Nikolic's MPs and admitted they were helped by some Zvornik folks. The MPs, Nikolic was able to identify who the soldiers were that helped them, and Vinko Pandurevic and Drago Nikolic prosecuted those Serb soldiers that assisted these guys by giving them a sandwich and telling them where the front line is. They prosecuted them for assisting the enemy and punished them. And you'll see the documents that support that. So we have the names of these four Muslim survivors. And you won't be surprised to hear that all four of those names are on the ICRC missing list, because after they were used as witnesses again the Serbs, they were executed. Maybe some day their bones will be identified and their loved ones will know that. Okay. We've got a little time left, and I don't want to take too much time tomorrow, so if you don't mind, I think I'll start with chapter 3, and -- which I call the linkage material. And with the help of Ms. Stewart, we'll go through that. And the first linkage material I want to talk about -- or the first person we'll talk about is General Miletic. And the first document I want to go to is a document you've seen part of. It's directive 7, the famous directive 7, where -- it was drafted by Miletic, where he wrote out the part about make life unbearable. Well, there's also a part at the very end which I believe Janet has marked for us regarding the logistic support for this operation, and -- I'm sorry, if I could take just one second to grab that. And I'm just read it briefly: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through a planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistic support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." They're making the Muslims dependent upon their goodwill, keeping the supplies to a minimum, yet not so bad that the international community is going to notice. You'll see the evidence to support exactly what they did. So this goes along with making life unbearable. And General Miletic played a major role in the convoys and what convoys went and what convoys didn't. And let's go now to an 18 June document. This is a June 18th called -- it's called an open message under the name of General Miletic from the Main Staff, and I'm not going to read it all to you, but it's talking about supplying the various materials to the enclaves. And in the end of it, General Miletic says, and this is -- you can see he's sending it to the Zvornik Brigade and the various brigades that have to do with the enclaves: "I demand a detailed check of all vehicles, including the inspection of cargo. Pay special attention to the fuel in the fuel tanks and the fuel being brought into the enclaves. Check the documents and the identity of all persons on board. Make a list of their names and their ID cards in order to ensure that the persons who enter the enclaves must leave the enclaves upon the completion of the task." Now, this shows that General Miletic is playing a very important role in this. Now, on its face there is nothing criminal about this, but it does indicate to us the role he's playing, and he can say to the Zvornik Brigade, "I demand a detailed..." Now, is that an order from a commander? No. Is it a directive you have to follow? Yes. This is consistent with Mladic's overall order directive 7 and the other materials that we've seen establishing the policy. And you'll see, speaking of fuel, how fuel was restricted and strangled. So by the time DutchBat was there in July when these events happened, they didn't have enough fuel to run their air conditioning or their electrical and they couldn't go out in vehicles. And this is all the Main Staff's doing through their corps, through their brigades, as it was done with General Miletic. Okay. One more, I think. The 13th July document. Now, this is an amazing document that was found recently in the Drina Corps collection, jammed in amongst a whole bunch of other telegrams and obviously missed by anybody going through this material. It's a communication authored by Lieutenant Colonel Milomir Savcic. Milomir Savcic is the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment. He is in a place called Borika, down by Zepa, where Tolimir has been stationed to look after the Zepa attack. And Savcic has received a proposal from Tolimir regarding all these massive amounts of prisoners that are being caught in the area of Nova Kasaba and Sandici, and so I want to look at every word on this one because we don't see many documents like this. It's entitled "Procedure for treatment of prisoners of war." "To the commander of the GS VRS." That's the Main Staff. That's of course Mladic, and for his information; assistant commander for religious and legal affairs, and for his information. We know who that is. That's Gvero. And the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. That's this guy Malinic who I mentioned to you that introduced a Dutchman to Beara. And it says: "Order. There are over 1.000 members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BiH army captured in the area of Dusanovo (Kasaba). Prisoners are under the control of the military police battalion of the 65th protection regiment." They have a unit there in Nova Kasaba, so it's natural that they have been the ones that have been dealing with all these prisoners. "Assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff" - of course we know who that is; Tolimir - "proposes the following measures: "Prohibit access to all unauthorised individuals, filming and photographing of prisoners. "Prohibit traffic for all United Nations vehicles en route to Zvornik, Vlasenica until further notice ... "Commander of the military police battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road, place them somewhere indoors or in an area protected from observation from the ground or the air." Now, these hundreds of prisoners, as I said before, are a great bargaining tool to receive for exchange, and the first thing you would want to do in that situation is bring in the ICRC, get these people registered, get them -- you can screen the ones that are military-aged men and get them taken care of. Why in the world would you hide them unless you had some nefarious activity? And let's look at who they're hiding them from. Perhaps you hide them from the Bosnian Muslim army that might try to break them out. But that's completely unrealistic. They are the Bosnian Muslim army. They're nowhere near the 2nd Corps forces at this point. There is no air force. There is no way that the Bosnian army can do anything about these guys. So who are they keeping them from when they're being observed from the ground or the air? The only people that are in the air in July of 1995 are NATO. They don't want these guys seen by NATO. They don't want the international community to know they exist. This is a very strong indication that the murder operation is in play. These people are to be hidden from the international community so they can be killed. Mr. Savcic was shown this document and wouldn't contest it but wouldn't acknowledge it, and I asked him who -- who should be -- who are they hiding these guys from, and he said, "Well, NATO." And I asked, well, why are they hiding them from NATO? And he thought about that for a bit and said, "Well, we would have been concerned that NATO mistook them for being Serbs and would have bombed them." And again, you can tell from an answer like that that he doesn't want to be anywhere near this, and it really tells us what this document's about. But then let's go on in the document. "Once the commander of the military police battalion receives this order, he shall contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the Main Staff." So we've got Tolimir involved in this, we've got Gvero involved in this, we've got Miletic involved in this, we've got Mladic involved. One document. We've got them all. So this is the line-up. This is the line-up for genocide. And it importantly shows who the important players are. Miletic is going to be issuing orders relating to these guys. This is an extremely important document to show you who was important, who is involved, and what they're up to. And I think this is probably the place where I need to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

Earlier on I mentioned an outstanding motion that was filed confidential and under seal relating to a request from the Prosecution for protective measures for different persons. However, if any names of witnesses are going to be mentioned in particular, then obviously we will need to go into private or closed session. I don't think there is a need to mention witnesses by name. You can actually refer to them the same way they have been referred in the motion itself, namely by reference to the pseudonym that was used in each case, in either or both of the previous cases, the Krstic and the Blagojevic one. Who is going to address? Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further submissions on the Prosecution motion? Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to seize the opportunity to raise one matter in the context of procedural matters which relates to the application of e-court in the courtroom. In the pending cases before the Tribunal, in -- at the point the Defence was to cross-examine a witness the Defence delivered the documents that it was going to use in cross-examination at the time when the witness was swearing in. We did not discuss these matters yet, and I move that the Trial Chamber issue a decision applying the same procedure that was applied in the Milutinovic et al. case, which is decision issued on the 16th of August, 2006; wherein it is stated that the Defence is duty-bound to upload into e-court all the documents that it will be using in the course of its cross-examination at the point when the witness is giving his solemn declaration from which point the Prosecution can no longer get in touch with the witness.
